nameStory: Eremosphaera gets its name from Greek words meaning 'desert sphere,' which perfectly describes these tiny, round green cells that often live alone in harsh conditions. The 'viridis' part simply means 'green' in Latin, though that might seem obvious for any plant!
description: Eremosphaera viridis is a microscopic single-celled green alga that you'll never see without a magnifying glass or microscope. Each cell is a perfect little green sphere, about the width of a human hair, living independently rather than forming colonies like many other algae. These tiny green orbs contain the same chlorophyll that makes trees green, but pack it all into one remarkable cell that does everything - eating, breathing, and reproducing - all on its own.

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Perfectly spherical cells that look like tiny green marbles under magnification, with no visible external structures or projections

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual cells measure about 50-100 micrometers across - roughly the thickness of a human hair and visible as tiny green specks with a strong hand lens

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to dark green coloration throughout the cell, sometimes appearing slightly yellowish-green in certain lighting

idTips.label: Growth pattern
idTips.description: Lives as isolated single cells rather than forming chains, films, or colonies like most other algae

idTips.label: Cell wall
idTips.description: Thick, smooth cell wall that gives the sphere a solid, marble-like appearance under magnification

habitat: Found in acidic, nutrient-poor waters throughout New England, particularly in bog pools, temporary puddles, and the edges of acidic ponds. These hardy little cells thrive in harsh conditions where other algae struggle, often appearing in shallow water that dries up periodically or in areas with fluctuating pH levels.

seasonality.spring: Most abundant as temperatures warm and temporary pools fill with snowmelt, appearing as faint green tints in otherwise clear water.
seasonality.summer: Continues to thrive in warm, shallow waters, often persisting even as pools begin to dry up and concentrate.
seasonality.fall: Still present but less noticeable as temperatures drop and metabolism slows, though cells remain viable.
seasonality.winter: Survives freezing by entering a dormant state, with cells remaining viable under ice or in dried sediments.

funFact: These microscopic green spheres are practically indestructible - they can survive being completely dried out for months, frozen solid, or exposed to extreme acidity, then spring back to life when conditions improve, making them some of nature's ultimate survivors.
confusionNotes: Under low magnification, single cells might be confused with other round green algae, but Eremosphaera's perfectly spherical shape and solitary lifestyle set it apart from colonial forms like Chlorella, which often cluster together and are slightly smaller.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an 'alga,' this organism is more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds, representing an ancient lineage that shows how plants first conquered harsh terrestrial environments billions of years ago.
compareHints: Since Eremosphaera is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other single-celled green algae in the same family. Unlike the more common Chlorella species, Eremosphaera cells are notably larger, perfectly spherical rather than slightly oval, and have much thicker cell walls that give them their distinctive marble-like appearance.
